This page explains the terms used in the app. Tap an entry to expand it. The question mark next to a control opens the matching entry directly.

1. You paste a YouTube link or share a video with SourceScribe.
2. “Check source” fetches the video metadata: title, length, available caption and audio tracks. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is sent to a provider yet.
3. You review the selection and start the job. Only this start allows the app to transfer audio.
4. The job continues in History even when you leave the app. The result is stored internally first and written to your export folder afterwards.

“YouTube only” uses just the captions YouTube itself offers. That costs nothing, needs no provider and usually finishes in seconds. Not every video has them, and automatic captions carry no punctuation and no speakers.

“YouTube, then STT” takes the captions when they exist and only otherwise uploads the audio to a provider. This is the frugal default.

“STT only” skips captions and always has the provider transcribe. Useful when you need punctuation, speaker separation or better quality.

“Both” produces two separate results for comparison and therefore costs one provider run.
Audio track: what the numbers mean

YouTube offers the same video in several audio renditions. Numbers such as 139, 140, 141, 249, 250 or 251 are YouTube-internal format numbers, not quality grades. Each stands for one combination of codec and data rate:

• The numbers 249, 250 and 251 are WebM files using the Opus codec.
• The numbers 139, 140 and 141 are M4A files using the AAC codec.
• Within one series the higher number means the higher data rate.

What data rate and size a track actually has is decided by YouTube per video, and the values shift over the years. SourceScribe therefore claims no fixed numbers; it shows codec, reported data rate and file size in plain words and suggests one track.

For transcription the smallest track is almost always enough. The reason is mechanical: before sending anything, the app re-encodes the chosen track to mono, 16 kHz, 64 kbit/s MP3, because speech-to-text services work at that resolution. A larger track adds no further information after that step, but it does cost more data and more download time.

The choice only matters when a video offers several languages, for example a dubbed version. Then the track decides which language gets transcribed. In that case the app asks instead of choosing for you.

Some videos also carry an audio description: a track in which a voice describes what happens on screen. SourceScribe marks it and never selects it on its own, because transcribing it would yield the picture description instead of the conversation.

DRC stands for dynamic range compression. For some videos YouTube additionally offers a rendition in which quiet passages are raised and loud ones lowered. It is meant for listening in noisy surroundings.\n\nFor transcription a DRC rendition has no demonstrated advantage and can raise background noise along with speech. SourceScribe therefore prefers the plain rendition and marks DRC tracks explicitly.

The codec describes how the sound was compressed: Opus is newer and slightly better than AAC at the same data rate. The container is the file form around it, so WebM or M4A.\n\nNeither matters for your result, because the app converts to MP3 before sending anyway. The values are shown so the choice stays traceable and can be recorded in the provenance.

The data rate in kbit/s says how many bits per second of sound are used. Data rate and video length give the approximate file size.\n\nWhen the size is prefixed with “approx.”, the value is an estimate: either YouTube only reported an approximation, or the app derived it from data rate and length. The file actually downloaded can differ.

“YouTube · provided by channel” means somebody uploaded or corrected the captions. These are usually the most accurate and contain punctuation.

“YouTube · auto-generated” is YouTube’s own speech recognition. Usually usable, but without punctuation, without speakers and with errors on names and technical terms.

“Automatically translated” is a machine translation of another track. SourceScribe leaves these out by default because they went through two machine steps and the errors add up. You can allow them under advanced options.

A provider is an external service that turns audio into text. SourceScribe has no server of its own; requests go straight from your device to the provider, with your own key and on your own bill.

AssemblyAI works asynchronously: the app uploads the audio, receives a job id and polls for progress. Offers speaker separation and word timings.

OpenAI and Groq work synchronously: the answer comes back on the request itself. Groq is usually cheap and fast.

Which options are actually possible depends on the chosen model, which is why unsupported switches are greyed out.

AssemblyAI runs separate locations. The choice in SourceScribe decides which address your request goes to, and therefore under which jurisdiction your audio is processed and stored. It is not a cosmetic label.

The decisive part: a key belongs to exactly one account and therefore to exactly one location. A key created in an EU account does not work against the US address and the other way round. So pick the same location you created the key in. If they do not match, the provider rejects the request with an authentication error.

SourceScribe stores the region with the key and binds it to the job, so a later change cannot move an existing job into a different jurisdiction unnoticed. The two locations offered here are the ones SourceScribe supports. Whether your account offers further locations is visible in your AssemblyAI account; SourceScribe cannot query that.

An API key is your personal password for a provider. You create it in the provider account and pay for usage through it.\n\nSourceScribe stores keys encrypted on this device, never shows them again in clear text and never writes them into logs, diagnostics or exports. A job only remembers the reference to the key. Deleting a key keeps old results, but waiting jobs need the key back.

Speaker separation, also called diarization, splits the transcript into passages per voice. The result then shows a label such as “A” or “B” in front of each passage.\n\nThis assigns voices, it does not identify people. The app invents no names. How reliable the separation is depends on the provider, the recording and the number of speakers. Not every model supports it.

Segment timings state where each paragraph starts in the video. That is enough for subtitles and for jumping back.

Word timings additionally give a time for every single word. That produces considerably more data and is only worth it if you want to cut or search word by word.

Without timings the SRT and VTT export formats are impossible, because subtitle files require times.

Enter words that occur in the audio and that speech recognition tends to spell wrong: proper names, company names, technical terms, abbreviations. The provider then prefers those spellings.\n\nOne line per term. This is a hint to the provider, not a guarantee. Not every model supports it.

The length limit is a guard against accidental cost: if the audio is longer than the configured value, the job stops before anything reaches the provider. The value applies per job and is part of the stored job configuration.

That is why the limit of a job that has already started cannot be raised afterwards. This is deliberate: a stored cost frame must not change by itself. To process a longer video, raise the limit before starting or prepare the job again with “Prepare again”.

The budget is a second, independent limit in US dollars. It is compared against the estimated cost of all submissions of the same job, including accepted and uncertain ones. Left blank, the app checks no cost limit.

The estimate shown is the same sum your budget is later checked against: the stored list price of the model plus the surcharges for speaker separation and key terms, counted per chunk and with the provider’s minimum billing, with the tariff date next to it. It is an orientation, not an invoice.\n\nIt contains no discounts, no retries and no provider price changes. When it says “Price unknown – no promise of free use”, SourceScribe has no verified tariff stored for that model; that is not an indication that it would be free. The provider invoice is always the binding one.

The conversion is done by SourceScribe on the device, not by the provider. The provider only ever returns one transcript; every format is produced from it locally. Choosing several formats produces one file per format from the same result. Nothing is transcribed again and nothing extra is charged.

• Markdown (.md): text with a heading and provenance fields. The default.
• Plain text (.txt): the text only, without a header.
• Structured data (.json): the complete result with times, speakers, provenance and warnings. For further processing.
• Subtitles (.srt) and web subtitles (.vtt): numbered blocks with time codes for video players. Only possible when the result contains times.
• “Original response (raw data)”: the unchanged provider answer. Only available when “Also keep raw data” is switched on.

The export folder is a folder of your choice outside the app that finished transcripts are written to. Android grants that permission per folder and remembers it permanently.\n\nIndependently of that, results always land inside the app first. A failed export therefore never deletes a result and never triggers a new billable request. If writing fails, for example because the folder was removed, you can pick another folder in History and save again.

Exported files are named after the video title, plus date, language and a short id so that two runs of the same source do not overwrite each other.\n\nYou can change the name in the result under “Actions” before exporting or sharing. Characters that file systems do not allow are replaced.

Both store a complete combination of settings: acquisition mode, provider, model, language, options, formats and limits.

“Save as default” makes the current combination the standard. Every new source starts from it afterwards. There is exactly one default.

A preset is an additional named combination, for example “Podcast with speakers” or “Fast and free”. Presets do not replace the default; you pick one deliberately on a new source. An upload approval is never stored with either: it is only created when you start a job.

“Queued”: scheduled, but not its turn yet.
“In progress”: currently working on the device.
“Waiting for network” or “Waiting due to rate limit”: the app holds back and retries later.
“Provider is processing”: the audio is with the provider, the result is still pending.
“Decision required”: the app stopped because something cannot be decided without you, for example a missing key or an exceeded length limit. The text underneath names the reason.
“Submission uncertain”: the request went out but the answer was lost. The provider may have accepted and billed it. SourceScribe never repeats such a request on its own.

For every result the app stores where it came from: source and video id, whether it came from YouTube captions or an external transcription, which model was requested and which the provider actually reported, which audio track was used and whether translation happened.\n\nThis is part of the export as well. The point is that months later you can still judge how much a transcript can carry, instead of treating it as verbatim.

“Only as technically required” deletes downloaded audio as soon as the step is done. The most frugal setting.
“Until the transcript is saved” keeps it until the result is persisted. The default, so an intermediate error does not force a new download.
“Keep permanently” leaves the audio in app storage until you delete the history entry. This can take a lot of space.

“Also keep raw data” stores the unchanged provider answer. Only then is the “Original response (raw data)” export format possible.

The storage limit is the ceiling SourceScribe imposes on itself in internal app storage: audio, intermediate files and results together. When it is reached the app stops the next step in a controlled way instead of filling the device. Results already stored are kept.\n\nParallel jobs decides how many sources are processed at the same time. More is not always faster: downloading and converting cost battery and CPU, and providers have rate limits of their own.

“Redacted” means blacked out: all content has been removed from the report beforehand. It contains technical values only, namely app and component versions, device properties, counters per job state and known error codes.\n\nIt contains no links, no titles, no transcripts and no keys. You see the full text before deciding whether to share it; without your sharing it does not leave the device.

The extraction component is the tool that fetches YouTube metadata, captions and audio: yt-dlp together with a JavaScript helper. YouTube changes its pages regularly, which is why this tool is updated far more often than the app itself. That is why SourceScribe can update it separately.

“Stable” is the regular release. “Nightly (preview)” is the day-to-day preview state: when YouTube has just changed something and the stable release has not caught up, nightly often already works, but it is less tested.

So when checking a source suddenly fails: check “Stable” first; if that does not help, check “Nightly (preview)”. When the app finds an update, put any public YouTube address into the field below. That makes the new version actually run before activation; it is only adopted when this functional test succeeds. Every version is additionally verified against its signature. “Restore previous engine” undoes an activation.

Python, the JavaScript runtime and FFmpeg are fixed inside the app and need an app update. Running jobs keep the version they started with.

In “YouTube only” mode, the only traffic leaving the device is the YouTube requests needed to load metadata and captions. No provider is involved.

As soon as an acquisition mode with STT is chosen and you start a job, the prepared audio file is transferred to the chosen provider. That never happens automatically and never without a chosen provider, model and key.

The app has no telemetry, no server of its own and no analytics. Keys stay on the device. A local cancel does not stop a request that already reached the provider.

STT is short for speech to text. It means automatic transcription: a service receives an audio track and returns the spoken words as text.

SourceScribe does not transcribe by itself. The app prepares the audio and sends it to a provider that you choose and pay for with your own key. That is why a provider, a model, a cost frame and a length limit appear wherever STT is involved.

Captions are the opposite case. They already exist as finished text at YouTube, cost nothing, and leave your device only as a request to YouTube. That is why “YouTube only” is the mode without a provider, without a key and without cost.

Resuming and retrying do not change this job’s limits: they belong to it permanently and form the cost frame you confirmed when you started it. Choose “Prepare again” to start the same link as a new job with a higher limit.
